title: Jacques Derrida
summary: Derrida invented “deconstruction” — a slow, attentive kind of reading that shows how every rigid opposition (reason and feeling, strong and weak, one’s own and the stranger’s) is in fact unstable, each side depending on the other. He showed that meaning is never fully “here and now”: it always carries traces of the past and an expectation of the future. In his later work he wrote about mourning, friendship, hospitality and forgiveness — about how to live with others, and with those who are gone.
onEmotions: Derrida never built a theory of emotions, but his concepts give feelings a subtle language. A feeling, like meaning, is never wholly “present”: it always holds a “trace” — a reference to something absent, to what has gone or has not yet arrived. Deconstruction is suspicious of hierarchies in which reason stands “above” feeling and joy is “more correct” than sorrow. And one more important thought: we are bound to other people — living or departed — by relationships that can never be completed, and that incompleteness is not a breakdown but a form of fidelity.

anxiety.text: For centuries translators of Plato stumbled over one word — pharmakon, which means both “remedy” and “poison” — and picked one meaning; in “Plato’s Pharmacy” Derrida showed that you can’t choose. Many things are built this way: they cannot be split into the purely good and the purely bad. The anxiety wearing you out right now, with nothing shameful in it, is probably a pharmakon too. It keeps you from sleeping and breathing, yet there is care in it as well: attention to what might happen, readiness for what matters. You don’t have to declare it your enemy, nor praise it. You can acknowledge its doubleness: “it gets in my way, and it is also looking out for me.” Sometimes that acknowledgment loosens its grip more than any attempt to switch the anxiety off.
anxiety.practice: Put a hand on your chest and say two sentences to your anxiety, like two meanings of one word: “You get in my way by…” and “You take care of me by…”. Don’t choose between them.

fear.text: “A specter is haunting Europe” — Derrida starts from this first line of the Manifesto in Specters of Marx and coins “hauntology,” from the French hanter, “to haunt.” The fear you can’t simply order away is much like such a visitor. A ghost is something that seems to be over but keeps coming back, or something that does not yet exist but already disturbs us. Many fears work exactly like this: they come from the past or from a possible future. Derrida suggested not exorcising the ghosts, not pretending they aren’t there, but learning to talk with them and to hear what they ask of us. You can ask your fear, the way one asks a ghost: where have you come from, and what are you trying to tell me? Sometimes a ghost that has been listened to stops being a threat and becomes a messenger.
fear.practice: Imagine your fear as a ghost standing in the doorway. Ask it under your breath, as Hamlet asked his father’s ghost: where have you come from, the past or the future, and what do you want of me? Listen without driving it away.

sadness.text: Reason above feeling, strength above weakness, joy above sorrow — Derrida noticed that Western thought loves pairs in which one half is always “the main one.” Your sadness doesn’t have to justify itself before that hierarchy. Deconstruction shows that the “lower” half is not simply subordinate but necessary to the first, and that the border between them is unstable. Extending Derrida’s thought, sadness is not a malfunction of some “normal” joyful state but part of the very fabric of feeling. Derrida also coined the word différance: it sounds like the French word for “difference” but is spelled with an “a,” and it means both “differing” and “deferring.” Meaning is never wholly here. Sadness is often about exactly this: about what points toward something absent.
sadness.practice: Write the word “sadness” in the middle of a page and draw arrows from it — to a person, a place, something that never came to be. This is your small web of traces: read it without drawing conclusions.

grief.text: Each time a friend died — Barthes, Foucault, Deleuze, Levinas — Derrida wrote a farewell text; later these texts became the book The Work of Mourning. Your grief, too, doesn’t have to keep to a correct timeline. Derrida argued against the idea of a “successful” mourning, after which the departed is fully “digested” and let go. Such success, Derrida thought, would in a sense be a betrayal. Fidelity to the one who is gone means keeping them as other, without appropriating them or dissolving them into yourself — and that can never be fully finished. One of his last books is titled Each Time Unique, the End of the World: the death of another is not an event in the world but the end of a whole world. Your grief is proportionate to that, and it doesn’t need to be hurried.
grief.practice: Recall one phrase of the person who is gone — in their words, with their intonation — and say it out loud. Let that voice go on sounding in you; there is no need to “close” it.

loneliness.text: “O my friends, there is no friend” — Derrida’s Politics of Friendship opens with this enigmatic sentence, attributed since antiquity to Aristotle. When you are lonely it can sound almost like a confession, and your longing for closeness is entirely real. Derrida, though, spends the whole book untangling the paradox. Friendship, in his view, always includes distance and asymmetry: even the closest person remains “wholly other,” with something in them you can never reach. Then loneliness is not just a failure of friendship but its secret part: we address friends who are not yet beside us, those who may still come. This doesn’t cancel the longing, but it makes it less a verdict and more an address — one that may still find an answer.
loneliness.practice: Send a short message today to someone you haven’t spoken to in a long while — no reason, just “I thought of you.” For Derrida, friendship is an address that may still find its answer.

quote.text: O my friends, there is no friend.
quote.author: Aristotle (a saying as reported by Diogenes Laertius and Montaigne)
quote.source: The leitmotif of Derrida’s Politics of Friendship (1994)

anger.text: Is it legal — and is it just? In “Force of Law,” Derrida insists that these are two different questions, and the anger boiling in you right now is most likely answering the second. Law is statutes, rules, procedures; they can be analyzed, criticized, changed. Justice is something more: it is always addressed to a single person in a singular situation, it is never fully embodied, it is always “to come.” Derrida would probably say that anger often flares in the gap between how things are arranged by the rules and what would be just. That gap is real, and your anger is not a whim. But justice, for Derrida, demands attention to the singularity of each person — including the one you are angry with. Anger can become the voice of justice as long as it doesn’t turn into a new rule with no exceptions.
anger.practice: Take three slow breaths out, then answer silently in one sentence: what justice, not yet realized, is my anger demanding — here, with this person?

shame.text: A philosopher stands naked while his cat silently looks at him — and he feels ashamed, and then ashamed of being ashamed in front of a cat. This is how Derrida opens the lecture “The Animal That Therefore I Am,” and what weighs on you now is of that same, deeply human kind. From this almost comic scene he draws a deep question: who is looking at me, and why do I feel I must hide something? The gaze of the other, Derrida says, can never be appropriated or fully understood. Extending Derrida’s thought, shame is a sign that you are open to another’s gaze, that you are not sealed off in yourself. Instead of fleeing shame, you can ask carefully: whose gaze is this — and must it be judging?
shame.practice: Meet the eyes of an animal, a face in a photograph, or your own reflection — for a minute, in silence. Notice: that gaze can be not a verdict but simply the presence of another, like the gaze of that cat.

guilt.text: “Forgiveness forgives only the unforgivable” — Derrida arrived at this almost impossible formula after years of thinking about forgiveness. The guilt you are carrying already shows how much other people matter to you. If we forgive only what is easy to forgive, that is not forgiveness but exchange: “you repented — I forgave you.” Genuine forgiveness, for Derrida, is unconditional, neither a deal nor therapy; that is why it is almost “impossible” — and yet it happens. A gentle conclusion follows: relief from guilt does not always have to be earned through endless atonement. Derrida distinguished unconditional forgiveness from conditional forgiveness — through apology, repair, conversation — and admitted that we live between the two. The second is available right now, and it is meaningful.
guilt.practice: Choose one step of conditional forgiveness — a short apology, a call, a small thing put right — and take it today. Leave the rest with time for now.

envy.text: If something needs supplementing, then it was never full to begin with — this is how Derrida, in Of Grammatology, describes the “logic of the supplement” (supplément). More broadly, Derrida criticized the “metaphysics of presence” — the belief that somewhere there exists a full, whole, self-sufficient being. Envy is a prickly, uncomfortable feeling, and it lives on exactly this belief: that the other has a fullness I lack. Deconstruction gently takes this picture apart: no one has fullness; every life is shot through with absence, deferral, lack. This doesn’t devalue what you want. But it lets you see that the person you envy also lives with incompleteness, perhaps invisible to you.
envy.practice: Imagine reading the life of the person you envy as a text — with margins, footnotes, crossed-out lines. What might lie outside the main text? And what “fullness” might someone see in you?

emptiness.text: There are spaces between the letters in this line, and without them you couldn’t read a single word: Derrida called such intervals “spacing” and considered the empty place a condition of writing. The emptiness and apathy you feel now are heavy, and they are not your fault. Derrida criticized the dream of a full, immediate meaning that would be wholly “here and now.” Meaning, in his view, always lives in a web of references: every word carries “traces” of other words, every experience points to others. The absence of fullness is not a breakdown but the condition of any meaning. Extending his thought, emptiness is not necessarily “nothing” but a pause in the text of a life. You don’t have to force yourself to feel; it is enough to notice the traces that still point to something.
emptiness.practice: Look at any page of text and rest your eyes not on the words but on the white gaps between them. Then look around: what one thing nearby still points you toward something dear? Just notice it.

quote.text: There is nothing outside of the text.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida

confusion.text: “Aporia” in Greek means, literally, “no passage,” a dead end — and Derrida believed that a real decision is possible only through just such an “ordeal of the undecidable.” If you are confused and can see no path, you may be standing right at that threshold. If everything is clear and calculable, that is not a decision but simply the application of a rule, like a calculator. You can truly decide only where you don’t know in advance what is right. For Derrida, confusion is not stupidity or weakness but honesty before a genuinely difficult situation in which two truths collide. It means you are not substituting a ready-made formula for a decision. You can bear it without rushing — and when the decision comes, it will truly be yours.
confusion.practice: Say aloud the two truths you are stuck between, and after each add: “and this is true too.” Don’t choose — let both be heard.

fatigue.text: To open the door to anyone who knocks, without asking their name or setting conditions — this is how Derrida described unconditional hospitality. If you are burned out, perhaps you have held such a door wide open for too long, and your exhaustion is a real limit, not a flaw of character. Derrida honestly admitted that in its pure form it is impossible: in real life hospitality needs conditions — a home, doors, rules, time. We always live between the unconditional ideal and the conditions without which it cannot be realized. Burnout probably comes when we try to live the unconditional without conditions: to be endlessly available, to answer everyone, to take everything in. Conditions — a door closed for the evening, a “not now” — are not a betrayal of your ideals but what allows them to go on living.
fatigue.practice: Close one “door” today, literally: turn off notifications for the evening or set an auto-reply saying “I’ll answer tomorrow.” That is a condition of hospitality, not a betrayal.

boredom.text: “I have forgotten my umbrella” — this phrase, in quotation marks and with no context at all, was found among Nietzsche’s papers, and in Spurs Derrida showed how hard it is to decide once and for all what it means. Boredom honestly reports that everything seems already read — yet even a single line turns out to be inexhaustible. Derrida was a master of reading in the margins: he carefully examined footnotes, asides, small details that others skipped. Deconstruction as a whole begins with noticing the unnoticed. Boredom probably arises when we read life only by its “main text,” its familiar plot. The margins — small things, accidents, oddities — are full of meanings waiting for attention.
boredom.practice: Step outside for five minutes and find a “marginalia” of the street — something nobody notices: a crack, a scrawl, a strange sound. Read it the way Derrida read Nietzsche’s umbrella.

joy.text: Derrida was often taken for a demolisher who takes everything apart, yet he kept saying that deconstruction is above all affirmation, a “yes.” He wrote that “yes” sounds before any question. Your joy needs no justification — at most, a second “yes.” In his writings on Joyce he reflected on the double “yes, yes”: the first “yes” is said to life, the second confirms it, repeats it, promises to keep that assent. Joy is that first “yes,” and the way to cherish it is the second: to remember, to repeat, to confirm. Joy in Derrida is not naive: it knows about fragility and finitude. But that is exactly why it is precious. You don’t have to hide it for fear it will end; you can affirm it twice.
joy.practice: Say aloud, briefly: “Yes — to this,” naming exactly what you are glad about. In the evening, say the same “yes” once more, as confirmation and promise.

love.text: In the documentary Derrida (2002), the philosopher is asked to say something about love; at first he answers that he has nothing to say, then he speaks of the difference between “who” and “what.” The tenderness in you now doesn’t have to find words either. Do we love a person — their singularity, a “someone” — or their qualities, a “something”: beauty, intelligence, kindness? Derrida admits that this distinction is never finally settled: love keeps wavering between the two. So tenderness doesn’t have to answer the question “what for.” Qualities can change and disappear, but what we love in a person as singular slips away from any list. That is its secret, not its flaw.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and silently say only their name — several times, slowly, without adding a single “because.” Notice what remains beyond any list.

gratitude.text: A present that is instantly repaid stops being a present — from this observation Derrida, in Given Time, builds his paradox: a true gift is almost impossible. The warmth of gratitude you feel now is not cancelled by this paradox; it is deepened. As soon as a gift is recognized as a gift, it enters an economy of exchange: the one who receives feels indebted, the one who gives expects something back. The circle of “given — returned” cancels the very gratuitousness of the gift. Derrida does not call on us to stop being grateful. The deepest gratitude is probably the kind that is in no hurry to pay off, that doesn’t turn a gift into a debt. It simply acknowledges: I was given something I could not have earned. And that acknowledgment is enough — with no obligation to return something of equal value right away.
gratitude.practice: Sit in silence for a minute, thinking of a gift you cannot and need not “return.” Don’t say thank you aloud or plan a gesture in return — just let it remain a gift.

hope.text: In French the future has two names: futur — what can be predicted and planned — and avenir, literally “what is coming,” the unexpected; all his life Derrida thought about the second. Your hope, even a quiet one, is turned toward it. In Specters of Marx he speaks of “messianicity without messianism”: an openness to what is to come without the promise of a particular savior or a ready-made picture of paradise. Hope, then, is not the certainty that everything will be fine but a preserved openness: a door left ajar for whatever may arrive. Derrida himself, in saying farewell, asked that words affirming life be passed on to those who came to his funeral. Hope, in this sense, is choosing life again and again.
hope.practice: Go to a window or a door, open it, and look outside for a minute without expecting anything in particular. This is avenir: a place left open for whatever may come.

quote.text: Always prefer life and constantly affirm survival.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: Farewell words read at his funeral (2004)

nostalgia.text: “I have only one language; it is not mine” — so begins Monolingualism of the Other, Derrida’s book about a childhood in Algeria and about a French that was both native and foreign to him. The nostalgia aching in you now speaks of what is dear — and not always of what was ever wholly yours. In an early essay, “Structure, Sign, and Play,” Derrida described two attitudes toward a lost origin: a sad, nostalgic one — longing for a lost center — and an affirmative, joyful acceptance that there never was a center and that the world is open to play. He did not demand that we choose one. Read with Derrida, nostalgia loves what was never wholly “ours” — and so it can live alongside openness to the new.
nostalgia.practice: Say aloud a word or saying from the language of your childhood — a household word, a grandmother’s phrase. Listen: it is yours and not quite yours — and still it has become part of you.

quote.text: I have only one language; it is not mine.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida

craving.text: In the 1989 interview “The Rhetoric of Drugs,” Derrida notes that the very notion of a “drug” is not purely medical: it mixes morality, politics, and a fear of the “artificial.” A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. Earlier, in “Plato’s Pharmacy,” Derrida had examined the Greek word pharmakon, which means both “remedy” and “poison.” He called neither for praise nor for simple condemnation — he proposed thinking slowly. The object of craving — a substance, a cigarette, a phone — works like a pharmakon: it promises relief and at the same time drains your strength. Craving shouts only about the “remedy.” You can calmly remember the other half of the word.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, breathe slowly and on each out-breath name both halves of the word to yourself: “this promises…” — “this takes away…”. Stay like this for a few minutes, until the wave eases a little.

addiction.text: “A dangerous supplement” — this is what Rousseau called something added to life to make up for a lack, which gradually begins to replace it; in Of Grammatology Derrida takes the phrase apart line by line. If your life has gradually arranged itself around one thing, that is a long-running circle, not a moral failure. In “The Rhetoric of Drugs,” Derrida notes that addicts are often condemned for “escaping reality” into an artificial world, and he shows that behind this condemnation stand old philosophical oppositions: “natural — artificial,” “authentic — fake.” In this light, addiction is a supplement that has taken up too much room. The useful question is not “why am I like this” but “what exactly is this making up for?” — loneliness, pain, emptiness, exhaustion.
addiction.practice: Say one sentence to someone you trust: “I think, for me, this makes up for…” Such a listener can also be a mutual-help group — people there know how to hear sentences like this.

hangover.text: Derrida titled one of his books Archive Fever: an archive is always incomplete, full of losses and erasures, and the wish to restore everything down to the last detail itself turns into a fever. No archive, however detailed, keeps everything. The morning after brings heaviness in the body, anxiety, shame, gaps in memory; all of it is agonizing, and you deserve gentleness. The morning attempt to reconstruct yesterday minute by minute is also archive fever: anxiety demands a complete record that will never exist. The past only ever reaches us as traces. You can acknowledge these gaps instead of filling them with the worst guesses, and, if needed, calmly ask people you trust — once you feel better.
hangover.practice: Sit down, rest your palms on your knees, and take a few slow breaths out. With each one, let go of one missing detail of yesterday: “I don’t remember this — and I’m not reconstructing it yet.”

euphoria.text: “At last, everything is here, whole!” — all his life Derrida took apart this dream of “full presence,” which philosophy has cherished since Plato. The high you are in now is a real experience, and you can treasure it. Derrida showed that any presence is always already shot through with “traces” of past and future. Euphoria is a rare moment when the dream of fullness feels almost fulfilled. That is no reason to debunk it. But it helps to remember the trace: this moment is precious not because it lasts forever but because it is already leaving an imprint in you, one you will be able to return to. Joy doesn’t have to last forever to be real.
euphoria.practice: Choose one detail of this moment — a sound, a color, a phrase — and give it a physical trace: take a photo, keep a ticket, fold down a page. You will be able to return to that trace.

crash.text: For Derrida, it isn’t only people we have to mourn: any loss — of a place, a time, a state — needs its own work of farewell. A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a substance — can feel like falling into a void, and it isn’t your fault. Then the comedown is a small mourning for the high that has passed. You don’t have to rush it or hide it. Derrida also coined the word différance, which fuses “difference” and “deferral”: meaning is never given all at once, it keeps being put off. Perhaps what felt complete at the peak will reveal its meaning later, in a calmer state. The drop doesn’t have to pass judgment on what was.
crash.practice: Say a short farewell to the high, out loud: “Thank you for…, I’m sorry it’s over.” Then do one simple thing that will support you today — a warm shower, a walk, a call.

panic.text: Not to rush toward a final reading — Derrida taught this all his life, and it is perhaps most needed in the minute when your body suddenly writes its frightening text. A pounding heart, a wave of terror, the sense that something irreparable is about to happen — you really are scared. Derrida distinguished two futures: futur — the predictable, the planned — and avenir — what arrives suddenly, without warning. Panic, extending his thought, is an encounter with the unexpected that comes not from outside but from within your own body. The thought “I’m about to lose my mind” is an attempt to read this wave at once as a final text. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it passes, you don’t need to interpret it — it is enough to lean on what is there: the floor, your breath, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and take a few slow breaths out, longer than the breath in. Then read the room like a text, one word at a time: name five objects out loud — just name them, without interpreting.

dread.text: “Is my death possible?” — Derrida takes up this question in Aporias and honestly finds no passage: finitude cannot be passed through and understood to the end. The abyss, the “what is it all for,” is a heavy feeling, and Derrida did not hide from it. And in his last interview, Learning to Live Finally, he speaks of “survival” (survivance) — not as something after life, but as life at its most intense, most alive, always bound up with others and with what we pass on to them: traces, words, care. The abyss, then, is not an answer but a place from which you can see especially clearly how precious life and our bonds with others are.
dread.practice: Tell one person today which trace of theirs lives on in you: a word, a habit, an act of care. This is Derrida’s “survival” — what we pass on to one another.

fomo.text: Somewhere there is a full, authentic life “as it really is,” without gaps or deferrals — Derrida called this belief the “metaphysics of presence” and took it apart all his life. The feed turns it into a daily feeling that truly gnaws, especially in the evening, scrolling through other people’s celebrations: for others, life is fully present; for me, there are only traces. Derrida would remind us that a trace is not second-rate: every life is made of traces, including the one on the screen. But their fullness is an effect too: snapshots, selected and arranged like any text. No one lives in full presence. Knowing this doesn’t devalue your life — it frees it from comparison with something that doesn’t exist.
fomo.practice: Imagine you are the editor of someone’s “perfect” picture: what did you cut so the frame would look like that? Then name one moment of your day that appeared in no feed at all.

sleepless.text: “The instant of decision is a madness”: Derrida quotes these words of Kierkegaard in “Force of Law,” reflecting on why a decision cannot be reduced to a calculation. And at three in the morning the mind keeps running through options, weighing, calculating — unable to stop, and truly exhausting. Derrida distinguishes calculation from decision. A calculation can be carried to the end if there is enough data. But a real decision, in his view, always passes through “the undecidable” — a moment when no knowledge guarantees the right answer. The nighttime mind is probably trying to calculate what cannot be calculated — to go through every option until the risk disappears. That is impossible not because of your weakness but because of the very nature of decisions. So at night you can stop calculating: morning won’t bring a full guarantee, but it will bring more strength.
sleepless.practice: Say silently to the question that keeps circling: “You can’t be solved by calculation. I’ll come back to you in the daytime.” Then count not options but out-breaths — from ten down to one.

betrayal.text: A promise that cannot be broken is no longer a promise but a forecast: Derrida showed that the possibility of not being kept is written into the very structure of every “I promise”: otherwise we would only promise what would happen anyway. This does not excuse the one who broke their word, and your pain is legitimate: betrayal breaks not only a bond but your trust in the world. But it explains why trust is always risky: to trust means opening yourself to someone who is truly other and cannot be controlled. So your trust was not naivety. It was courage, without which no bond is possible — and that courage remains yours.
betrayal.practice: Say aloud: “I trusted because…” — and finish the sentence. Listen to what that reason says about your courage.

jealousy.text: “A letter always arrives at its destination,” Lacan claimed; “a letter can always fail to arrive” — get lost, reach the wrong person, be understood differently — Derrida replied in The Post Card. Jealousy is agonizing precisely because every sign, glance or delayed reply becomes a letter you don’t know how to read. Each such sign is a painful encounter with that “undecidability”: another person’s signs never give a full guarantee; they can always be read in different ways. This is not something abnormal in you but the condition of loving a living, separate person. Relief may come not from a final decoding but from accepting that there won’t be one — and from a direct, honest conversation instead of interpretation.
jealousy.practice: Take one troubling sign and silently read it in three different voices — jealous, indifferent, tender. Notice that you don’t know which reading is true — and that you can simply ask.

resentment.text: When, in the late 1990s, the world filled up with reconciliation commissions and public repentance, Derrida objected unexpectedly in “On Forgiveness”: true forgiveness cannot be an obligation. An old grudge, carried for years, is heavy, and it speaks of a real wound. If forgiveness is demanded, bought with apologies, turned into a procedure of “reconciliation,” it stops being forgiveness and becomes a deal. Forgiveness, for Derrida, is an unconditional gift, possible only as something exceptional. So you are not obliged to forgive on schedule, and your grudge is not a moral failure. But holding on to it is not a duty either. Between “forgive” and “never forgive” there is a space: to acknowledge the wound, to remember it — and yet gradually stop giving it the central place in your life.
resentment.practice: Choose one small thing the grudge controls today — a route, a song, a thought before sleep — and take it back. You don’t have to forgive to do this.

heartbreak.text: The first part of Derrida’s The Post Card, “Envois,” is written as love letters to an unnamed addressee — full of distance, uncertainty and the fear that the letter won’t arrive. When the person is alive but has left your life, the heart hurts almost physically, and that is a loss of its own kind. For Derrida, any relationship with another carries the possibility of separation from the very beginning: we are bound to the other precisely as someone separate, someone who can leave. A breakup, though, does not cancel what was: the relationship leaves a “trace” that goes on living in you — in words, habits, ways of seeing. You don’t need to erase that trace by force or keep it as a shrine. You can allow yourself sadness and allow the other to remain other — not possessed, but not crossed out either.
heartbreak.practice: Imagine sending this person an “envoi” you will never post — a single sentence. Say it to yourself and let it go, like a letter that may never arrive.

impostor.text: Your signature works only because it can be repeated — Derrida examines this oddity in “Signature Event Context.” The fear of being exposed as “not the real thing” speaks more often of how demanding you are of yourself than of any actual fakery, and this fear is exhausting. All authenticity rests on repetition, imitation, citation. Each of us learns to speak, write and work by repeating others — what Derrida called “iterability.” The inner “impostor” starts from a myth of the pure original — of people who “truly” know how to do everything on their own. There are no such people. Relying on what you have learned from others is not deception but the condition of any skill.
impostor.practice: Sign your name three times in a row and compare the signatures: none matches the others exactly, and all are yours. Then name three people from whom you learned your craft.

self_hatred.text: Sometimes the body’s defense system begins to attack the body itself — this is called autoimmunity, and in his late work Derrida turned the word into a philosophical concept. Self-hatred is a very heavy experience, and its voice does not tell the truth about you. The inner critic probably resembles such a mechanism: once, perhaps, it was meant to protect you from mistakes, rejection, shame, but now it strikes at what it should be protecting. Deconstruction also teaches distrust of rigid oppositions: “worthy — worthless,” “strong — weak.” The critic speaks in exactly such binary verdicts. Instead of refuting them on the spot, you can notice that they are too simple for a living person.
self_hatred.practice: Say one of the critic’s phrases out loud — then ask it, as you would ask a friend: “What were you once trying to protect me from?” Answer it in the tone you would use with someone close.

helplessness.text: A pure gift expects nothing in return, true forgiveness forgives the unforgivable, true justice cannot be reduced to a rule — so Derrida called them “impossible,” and precisely in this “experience of the impossible” he saw the place where responsibility begins, not where it ends. The sense that you can’t change anything is heavy, and it often reflects real circumstances rather than your weakness. A gentle but important conclusion follows: the fact that you can’t solve everything doesn’t make your small responses meaningless. Helplessness is not a verdict on your strength but an encounter with its limit; and right at that limit you can still respond — with attention, a word, your presence.
helplessness.practice: Choose the smallest action available to you right now — a message, a glass of water for someone, one word of support — and do it within five minutes. This is a response at the very border.

procrastination.text: A preface is written last but placed first: in Dissemination Derrida ironically examines this habit books have of beginning with what was written at the end. If you just can’t get started, it is draining, and it isn’t laziness. Derrida coined the word différance: in French it sounds exactly like différence, “difference,” but it also carries the sense of “putting off.” Meaning, for Derrida, is always deferred: it is never given at once and in full. There is never a full, ready-made meaning at the start of any work — and putting things off is often fed by the expectation that you can begin only once everything is clear. In Dissemination, Derrida ironically examines prefaces: they are written last, even though they are placed first. So you don’t have to start at the beginning — clarity will come as you work.
procrastination.practice: Write for five minutes “from the middle”: any piece of the task, deliberately imperfect. The preface, as with Derrida, will come later.

uprooted.text: At twelve, Derrida was expelled from his school in Algeria: the Vichy regime had stripped Jews of French citizenship. Being cut off from home — a move, emigration, losing your ground — is a real loss, and he knew it from the inside. Later he wrote Of Hospitality and noted that the French word hôte means both “host” and “guest”: the same people trade places. Someone who has moved lives in this doubleness: in the new place they are a guest, but gradually they also become a host — of their own corner, language, habits — and one day they welcome others. The feeling of “not quite belonging” is not a flaw but a special knowledge that those who never left don’t have.
uprooted.practice: Walk your “host’s” route today — somewhere you already know the way without a map — and along the way notice one place where you are still a guest. Both positions are legitimate.

overload.text: “Artifactuality” is a word Derrida coined in conversations with Bernard Stiegler (Echographies of Television): the events of the day don’t simply happen — they are made, selected, edited and delivered at a certain rhythm. The feed, notifications and endless news are exhausting, and it isn’t a personal weakness: this stream is made so that it never ends. Overload is an encounter not with the world as such but with an enormous production of messages about the world, designed for your attention. Derrida didn’t call for turning away from events, but he insisted on slow, critical reading. And slow reading takes time and pause. Switching off the stream for a while is not escape but the condition of attentiveness.
overload.practice: Choose one news item or post and read it slowly, aloud, like a text: who made it, what was selected, what was left out of the frame. Let the rest of the stream wait.

unreality.text: “I hear myself speak” — what could be closer? In Voice and Phenomenon Derrida showed that even this is never given to us whole and instantly: it is mediated by signs, memory, a tiny delay. When the world or you yourself seem unreal, it is strange and frightening, and it deserves careful handling. Full, hundred-percent presence is an ideal, not the norm, and in moments of unreality you simply feel acutely a gap that everyone has. This doesn’t mean the world has vanished. Its traces remain: the weight of objects, sound, touch. You can return to them without demanding that reality be completely solid.
unreality.practice: Touch three different surfaces near you and name them aloud: smooth, warm, rough. These are traces of the world that need no proof.

awe.text: “The colossal” — Kant’s name for what is almost too large for our perception — gets a whole chapter in Derrida’s The Truth in Painting. Mountains, the sea, a cathedral, the night sky: awe before them is precious, worth simply savoring. Kant wrote that in such moments the imagination cannot take in the whole, and this is at once unsettling and elevating. Derrida carefully shows that the sublime lives at the border, at the very edge of our capacity to grasp. Awe, then, is an encounter with the “almost too big” that fits into no frame. You don’t need to explain it or photograph it: you can let it remain a little larger than you are able to hold.
awe.practice: Stand for a minute before whatever stirred your awe, without taking a photo. Notice where your capacity to take it in with your eyes runs out.

relief.text: Hegel’s Aufhebung — “sublation,” in which something is at once cancelled, preserved and raised higher — Derrida proposed translating with the French relève: both “lifting up” and “the changing of the guard.” Derrida loved such double-bottomed words, where one movement both cancels and preserves. When things finally let go and you can breathe out, it deserves to be noticed: you held the tension for a long time. Relief is like such a changing of the guard: the tension doesn’t simply disappear, it hands over its post but leaves experience in you. Now you know that you held out. You don’t need to look for the next worry right away or hurry on. You can let yourself stand in this minute when the guard has changed.
relief.practice: Name in one sentence exactly what you held out through. Take three slow breaths out, noting to yourself: “post handed over.”

calm.text: Plato’s Timaeus contains an enigmatic word, khōra — a place that receives everything that appears in it but coincides with none of it and holds on to nothing; Derrida devoted a 1993 essay to it. The calm you are in now is not emptiness but an open state, and it is good simply to be in it. Calm resembles khōra: not an absence of thoughts and feelings but the capacity to give them room without clutching at any of them. Everything passes through you, and you remain spacious. Such calm doesn’t have to be earned or used for anything — it is valuable in itself.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing thoughts and sounds as things passing through a space, and hold on to none of them.

inspiration.text: “Invention of the other” — in the essay “Psyche,” Derrida plays on the double sense of this phrase: we invent the new, but the other also, as it were, invents us, arriving from outside. What is coming to you now as if on its own is a joyful and somewhat mysterious state, worth treasuring without rushing to explain it. A true invention, in his view, cannot be fully programmed — it is always a bit of a “newcomer,” an unexpected guest. Inspiration is a visit that cannot be summoned on command but can be met with hospitality. You don’t need to claim it as a personal achievement or fear that it will leave. Better to write down what has come while the guest is here — and leave the door open.
inspiration.practice: Write down everything that has come, without editing, while the guest is here. At the end leave an empty line for whatever else may knock.

schadenfreude.text: Rousseau considered compassion the most natural, “pure” feeling, but Derrida, reading him in Of Grammatology, noticed that even compassion requires imagination — comparing yourself with another, putting yourself in their place. A secret joy when something goes wrong for someone else is familiar to almost everyone, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. And where there is comparison, its shadow is always close by. Schadenfreude and sympathy are not the opposites of a “good” and a “spoiled” heart but two sides of one movement: we measure ourselves against others. Someone else’s failure seems for a moment to confirm your place. Knowing this doesn’t commit you to gloating, but it frees you from shame over the mere fact of the feeling and lets you ask: what comparison is occupying me so strongly right now?
schadenfreude.practice: For half a minute, silently trade places with the person who failed. What do you feel from that side of the comparison — and what does it say about your own tiredness or insecurity?

contempt.text: “Us” and “them,” serious and frivolous: Derrida’s deconstruction begins by noticing how one term in a pair is quietly placed above the other. Contempt is a cold, “looking down” feeling, and it often protects something very vulnerable. Derrida shows that such a hierarchy is held in place by violence: the “lower” term is needed so that the “higher” can define itself at all. Contempt is a hierarchy built inside the soul: for me to be “normal,” “worthy,” someone has to end up below. Sometimes there is real pain or hurt in this. But it helps to notice how much the “high” depends on the “low.” Then contempt need not be suppressed but can be read: what exactly am I trying so hard to separate from myself?
contempt.practice: Silently name a quality that arouses your contempt, and flip the pair: what if the “low” is needed so that the “high” in me can define itself at all? Where is that quality — or the fear of it — in me?

disgust.text: Kant is willing to let almost anything into art — furies, diseases, the devastation of war — except the disgusting; in the essay “Economimesis” Derrida notes that everything else can be “digested” into a beautiful image, but this cannot, and the system expels it in order to stay whole. Disgust is a strong, almost bodily reaction, an ancient defense of body and soul, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. It — whether toward people, a situation, or yourself — marks the border of what you can take in right now. That border is not eternal and doesn’t necessarily say anything about the worth of what is rejected. It is enough to notice it, without turning it into a final verdict on either the other or yourself.
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust lives, and breathe out slowly right into that place. Ask yourself silently: “What exactly can I not let into myself right now?” — and simply hear the answer.

revenge.text: Friend or enemy? For the jurist Carl Schmitt, politics began with this distinction; in Politics of Friendship Derrida showed that the border is never final: an enemy may be a former friend, and a friend can wound more deeply than an enemy. You were hurt, and the sense of injustice inside is demanding an outlet. The thirst for revenge tries to fix the other permanently in the role of enemy — and in doing so chains you to them as well. At the same time, the demand for justice in it is real: what happened must be acknowledged. You can respect that demand without handing it the wheel. A revenge fantasy is a signal of a wound, not a plan of action; hearing the signal is already a step toward getting your freedom back.
revenge.practice: Walk for a few minutes and ask yourself as you go: what do I actually want — acknowledgment, an apology, safety, distance? Which of these steps requires no one’s pain?

anger_at_loved.text: In Latin, hostis — stranger, enemy — and hospes — guest, host — share a root, and from this kinship Derrida coined the word hostipitalité, “hostipitality.” Anger at those closest to you can be especially sharp, and you feel ashamed of it afterward, but it does not cancel love. He shows that hospitality always carries tension: in welcoming another, we give up our space, time, strength to them, and the host sometimes feels like a hostage. Intimacy is the deepest kind of hospitality, and so flashes of hostility within it are inevitable. Anger here often says: my boundaries have worn thin. You don’t need to pour it out on the other person — you can hear it as a request for room for yourself.
anger_at_loved.practice: Give yourself ten minutes today of what you are missing — quiet, a walk, a closed door. A host, too, needs a corner where no guests are received.

ambivalence.text: “I am at war with myself,” Derrida admitted in one of his last interviews. Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard and confusing, but it is a very honest state. All his life Derrida worked with what he called the “double bind”: situations in which two opposite demands are equally legitimate and neither cancels the other. He was in no hurry to reconcile them, because a hasty synthesis usually suppresses one side. Mixed feelings toward someone close are not a mistake to be fixed by choosing “I really love them” or “I really hate them.” Both feelings tell the truth about different sides of the bond. You can hold them together without demanding a final verdict of yourself.
ambivalence.practice: Hold an object in each hand: one hand is “what I love in them,” the other “what I can’t stand.” Hold both for a minute without lowering either.

quote.text: I am at war with myself.
quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: Interview with Le Monde (2004), published under the title “I Am at War with Myself”

guilty_relief.text: One of two friends will almost certainly outlive the other and mourn them — Derrida called this the “law of friendship” and believed it is at work from the very first meeting. That is why relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening — yet relief and love can live side by side. Loss is written into every bond from the very beginning, and anticipating it becomes part of love itself. A long farewell — an illness, a difficult relationship — begins mourning before the end. So relief doesn’t mean there was no love: you may have been carrying both grief and strain for a long time. Relief is not betrayal but the exhale of someone who has held a heavy load for a long time.
guilty_relief.practice: Say two sentences in a low voice, one after the other: “I feel relieved because…” and “And I still love…”. Don’t choose between them — let them stand side by side.

indifference.text: Meaning, Derrida said, never arrives on time: it is always late, showing up afterward, through traces. Sometimes you aren’t moved by what you “should” be — someone else’s grief, a celebration, important news — and guilt about your indifference arrives right away. Derrida coined the word différance (with an “a” instead of an “e”), joining two senses of the French verb différer: “to differ” and “to defer.” So feeling, too, doesn’t have to show up on schedule. The lack of a response now doesn’t prove you don’t care: the experience may be deferred, muffled by tiredness or by self-protection, or it may come by another path. The demand “feel the right thing right now” is a program, not a response. Allow yourself not to perform a feeling, and see what comes later.
indifference.practice: Don’t perform anything for five minutes: sit without demanding the “right” feeling of yourself. Just notice what is there instead — even if it is tiredness or emptiness.

escape.text: Destinerrance — Derrida built this word from destination (address, destiny) and errance (wandering): any letter may fail to reach its addressee, go astray, end up with someone else. The wish to drop everything and go where no one knows you says that your present life has grown cramped. So it is with us: no single role defines us once and for all. The wish to run away is your “wandering letter”: part of you doesn’t match the address at which you currently live. This doesn’t require an immediate escape, but it isn’t worth silencing that voice either. You can ask where exactly it is calling you and which “I” in you doesn’t fit into your current role.
escape.practice: Turn off your usual route today — one unfamiliar street, a different entrance, another stop. Let the “wandering letter” travel a little toward its own address.

forbidden_attraction.text: “There is something secret here” — Derrida keeps returning to this in Passions: in every other there is something that is never fully revealed, and it is precisely this inaccessibility that draws us. Attraction to someone unavailable or “the wrong person” brings turmoil and shame, but the feeling itself is not a wrongdoing. Derrida insisted that the secret doesn’t need to be exposed or reduced to a simple explanation. Forbidden attraction shows how desire reaches toward the other precisely as other — toward what cannot be possessed. Perhaps in this person you recognize something you lack: liveliness, freedom, a different life. You don’t need to pass judgment on yourself or rush to a decision. You can treat the secret with respect — your own as well — and ask what this desire is saying.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Sit with this feeling for a minute, deciding nothing and doing nothing, as you would beside someone else’s secret. Then silently name one quality of this person that you would like to develop more in your own life.

social_anxiety.text: Anyone can quote, repeat and read any word of yours in a context you never intended — Derrida called this “iterability.” When fear of other people’s judgment turns every sentence into an exam, it is exhausting, and holding on like that for a whole evening is very hard. It follows that no one fully controls how they will be understood. Social anxiety is a desperate attempt to keep hold of every possible reading of yourself. But that task is impossible for anyone, even the most confident person. There is relief in this: if perception can’t be fully controlled, you can stop trying. Your words will be read in different ways — and that isn’t your mistake, it is how all speech works.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, let yourself say one sentence without checking how it will be taken — just say it. I will be read in different ways: that is how all speech works.

uncertainty.text: A decision that can be calculated is no longer a decision but the running of a program: so in “Force of Law” Derrida argues that a real decision is possible only in “the undecidable,” where no rule guarantees the answer. You want to know what will happen, and you can’t, and that really is hard. Uncertainty, then, is not a breakdown in your life but the condition for anything in it being decided and happening at all. That doesn’t make it pleasant, but it changes its meaning: you don’t have to know everything in advance in order to act. You can take the next small step, acknowledging that it is taken “at the edge” of knowledge — as are most important steps, for everyone.
uncertainty.practice: Take one small step right now “at the edge of knowledge” — send the email, make the call, open the file you need — without waiting for clarity. Tell yourself: “I don’t know how it will turn out, and still I go.”

waiting.text: A man comes to the door of the law, the doorkeeper says “not yet,” and the man waits at that door his whole life — Derrida devoted his essay “Before the Law” to this parable of Kafka’s. Waiting — for an answer, results, news — also stretches time and keeps you from living in the present. At the end he learns that the door was meant for him alone. Derrida reads the parable as a story of how waiting can become one’s entire life if it is given all one’s attention. Your waiting is legitimate, but it doesn’t have to fill the whole space. The door will open or it won’t, and that is not always in your power. But whether you sit motionless by the door — that, in part, is. You can wait while continuing to live beside the door.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, do something unrelated to what you are waiting for — and step away from the “door” literally: leave your phone in another room. “I am waiting — and living at the same time.”

regret.text: “I would like to learn to live finally” — so begins Derrida’s Specters of Marx, and learning to live, in his view, is possible only in conversation with ghosts. Regret over what you did or didn’t do also returns again and again, like an intrusive guest. There Derrida coined the word “hauntology” — from the French hanter, “to haunt.” The past, in his view, does not vanish without a trace: it returns as ghosts with whom we have to speak. Regret is such a ghost: a path not taken or a word that can’t be taken back. There is no use driving it out by force, but you can listen to it. Often the ghost comes with a question: what truly matters to you? The answer can become not a verdict on the past but a hint for the future.
regret.practice: Write a short letter from the “ghost” of your regret to you — three or four lines: what does it want to say about what matters to you now?

longing.text: “The world is gone, I must carry you” — Derrida reads this line by Paul Celan slowly, closely, in Rams. Missing a particular person — their voice, their habits, their presence — can be almost physical. Derrida sees in this line the essence of our bond with an other who is not beside us: when the other is far away or gone, we carry them within us — in memory, in words, in a way of seeing the world. Longing is the very feeling of this burden, its weight. It is heavy, but it also bears witness to the bond: you carry the person because they are dear to you. You don’t need to strive to “stop missing them.” You can notice how exactly you carry them, and let this be a form of fidelity, not only of pain.
longing.practice: Read Celan’s line aloud: “The world is gone, I must carry you.” Then do something small and warm today in this person’s spirit.

world_pain.text: How can I justify feeding my cat when so many cats in the world go hungry? Derrida asks this uncomfortable question in The Gift of Death: in responding to one, I fail at that same moment to respond to countless others. Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can weigh you down, and it speaks of your sensitivity. No one can answer all the pain of the world at once. Guilt over “insufficient” care for the world is not a sign of your callousness but part of the human condition. It is no reason to turn away, but it is a reason to let go of the demand to be responsible for everything. You can choose one concrete response — attention, help, a word — and recognize that it is meaningful, even if it doesn’t cover everything.
world_pain.practice: Do one concrete thing today for one person — support someone with a word or a deed. Then put the news aside for a minute and just look out the window.

quote.author: Jacques Derrida
quote.source: The Gift of Death (1992); in the French original, “Tout autre est tout autre”

rejection.text: Consent that could not have been withheld is not consent but an automaton: this is how Derrida, in “Ulysses Gramophone,” reads Joyce’s final “yes,” the word on which the novel ends. A refusal wounds painfully: it feels as if you have been told “no” entirely, to the whole of you, not to one request. The other’s freedom to refuse is the condition for their “yes” ever meaning anything. Refusal is a bitter but inseparable side of the other’s freedom, not a verdict on your worth. It speaks of a meeting of two freedoms that, this time, did not coincide. The pain doesn’t disappear, but it stops being proof that something is wrong with you.
rejection.practice: Read aloud: “This person (or place) is free to say ‘no’ to me. This ‘no’ is about them and the situation, not about the whole of me.” Read it once more — more slowly.

abandonment.text: In some parts of France adieu is said not only on parting but also on meeting — Derrida recalls this in his farewell address Adieu to Emmanuel Levinas. The fear of being abandoned can poison even good relationships, and it often grows out of old wounds that deserve gentleness. So every “hello” already holds a “farewell”: meeting another acknowledges from the very start their separateness and freedom. Your fear senses this truth about every bond acutely. But what follows from it is not only anxiety: since the other is free to leave, their presence beside you is each time a gift, not an obligation. Today they are here, and you can notice that.
abandonment.practice: Say your “hello” to someone close today a little more attentively than usual — and notice one sign that they are here: a gesture, a word, a message.

unrequited.text: Can anything be given without expecting something in return? In Given Time Derrida answers that a true gift can hardly be written into an exchange: as soon as I expect a return, it becomes a deal. You give your feeling and receive silence or a polite refusal, and that hurts. A gift in the strict sense is what is given without demanding anything back. Your love, left unanswered, is not a failed deal but perhaps the closest thing to a gift there is. This doesn’t cancel the pain or the wish for reciprocity, and you don’t need to give those up. But you can see that the feeling you experienced has value in itself, not only as an investment that ought to pay off.
unrequited.practice: Close your eyes and spend a minute with what this love has revealed in you: what you are capable of feeling, noticing, giving. That remains yours, even without an answer.

humiliation.text: Every name is already a little violent: a label cuts a person out of their complexity and pins them in place — in Of Grammatology Derrida called this the “originary violence” of naming. Being humiliated, as if reduced to something small and put on display, is one of the most painful experiences. Humiliation is an extreme form of this violence: another tries to fix a single definition to you — “pathetic,” “ridiculous,” “nobody.” Such a definition is never the last word. Meaning, he said, always escapes final fixing; all the more so a person. A humiliating scene is one text about you, read by one reader — not the whole truth. You are still more than what you were called.
humiliation.practice: Write the label that was pinned on you in the middle of a page, and around it three other facts about yourself that it cannot contain. See how little room it takes up now.

body_shame.text: When drawing a self-portrait, an artist cannot look at themselves and at the page at the same time — so, Derrida noticed, every self-portrait is partly drawn blind. Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and it deserves gentleness, not criticism. Derrida curated an exhibition at the Louvre and wrote the book Memoirs of the Blind — about drawings and self-portraits. We never see ourselves whole and directly — only in a mirror, in a photo, through other people’s eyes. Your image of your body is a self-portrait too, drawn partly blind, dictated by other people’s gazes and pictures. It doesn’t coincide with the living body that breathes, feels, and holds you in the world. You can trust this portrait a little less — and the body itself a little more.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes and describe your body not by how it looks but by how it feels: warmth, breath, support, the touch of your clothes. What is it doing for you right now?

illness.text: Learning to Live Finally is the title of Derrida’s last major interview, given when he was already seriously ill; in it he admits that he never learned to live, and goes on learning. When illness lets your body down, it is hard both physically and emotionally: plans collapse, and you have to depend on others. Derrida spoke of “survival” (survie) — and insisted that this is not a pitiful remnant of life but life itself in its intense, most living form: to live is always to live “beyond,” in spite of. A time of illness is not a pause in “real” life but life too, with its own discoveries, bonds and affirmations. You don’t need to put on a show of cheerfulness. But each day still holds something you can affirm: a conversation, a taste, a thought, someone’s hand.
illness.practice: Choose one small thing you can affirm today — a favorite cup, a window, someone’s voice on the phone — and give it five whole minutes. Let this be your “yes” to the day.

pride.text: The final signature on a text is set not by the author but by “the ear of the other” — Derrida makes this unexpected claim in Otobiographies, reading Nietzsche. Pride in what you have done is a deserved and healthy feeling, worth enjoying without reservations. What we make comes alive when someone responds to it, “countersigns” it. Pride is doubly good when you notice both signatures: your own — effort, courage, work — and those of the people who received it, helped, and rejoiced with you. This doesn’t diminish your achievement but makes it alive and shared. Pride doesn’t have to be modest or solitary: you can celebrate it, recognizing both yourself and those beside you.
pride.practice: Say out loud what exactly you have done. Then call or message one person who responded to it — let them add their “countersignature” next to yours.

melancholy.text: Il y a là cendre — “cinders there are”: for many years Derrida kept returning to this phrase. Bright sadness is a quiet feeling with no misfortune in it, only tenderness toward what is gone and fragile, and it doesn’t need to be “cured.” In the small book Cinders (Feu la cendre, 1987) he reflects on ash as the most fragile of traces: of what was, almost nothing remains, and yet this “almost nothing” is here, and it can be noticed. Melancholy is attention to such traces: the smell of autumn, an old photograph, time gone by. It doesn’t demand the return of the past, nor does it seek to forget it. It is a way of keeping what no longer exists with a light touch — and there is a beauty of its own in that.
melancholy.practice: Find some “cinders” around you — a small trace of the past: an object, a smell, a sound. Sit with it for a minute, doing nothing.
